progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From C01: skeletal formulas and implied hydrogens (a carbon in a C=C has one fewer H); the longest chain containing the multiple bond; numbering from the end nearer the multiple bond, which beats branches because it is named in the ending; methyl and ethyl; halogens as prefixes with locants (c04a). From C02: structural isomers; chain (skeleton changes), position (group moves on the same skeleton), functional group (different family); "if the skeleton and the position both change, they are chain isomers" (c02 author note d). From C03: general formulas CnH2n+2, CnH2n, CnH2n−2. From C04a: addition, one piece on each carbon, one product; HX with an alkene at room temperature, no catalyst; an unsymmetrical alkene gives two possible products. From C04b: substitution with UV light, one H swapped, HX as the second product, a mixture of positions; UV light is an energy source; an alkyne adds twice, and "excess" means both steps; bromine water is decolourised by alkenes and alkynes at room temperature without UV light, not by alkanes; for an open-chain hydrocarbon with one multiple bond, the formula decides which. From P02 (the last video): what the bromine water test looks like in the lab. Not assumed: any other family.
progression.startsWith: An unseen hydrocarbon question. The video opens: A hydrocarbon question can ask you to name a molecule, sort its isomers, or predict what it makes.
progression.stopsAfter: naming two skeletal alkenes, numbering from the end nearer the double bond, and classifying them as chain isomers with a reason; identifying addition and substitution from the bonds and conditions, and writing an equation for one product of each; identifying an alkyne from its tetrachloro addition product by counting and placing the added atoms; evaluating a bromine water conclusion with the molecular formula.
progression.nextLesson: how an O–H group changes alcohol properties (route chem-m7-c05).

teaching.task: Given a skeletal formula, a molecular formula, a reagent or a test result, how do you name a hydrocarbon, sort its isomers, and predict or work back through its reactions?
teaching.causalExplanation: Why B is numbered from the right: the double bond is named in the ending, so it gets the low number first (2b, 2d). Why each alkene is C₆H₁₂: one double bond removes two hydrogens (2c). Why A and B are chain isomers: same formula and family, different skeleton (2c). Why pent-2-ene adds: a double bond opens and no light is needed (3b). Why pent-2-ene gives two possible products: unsymmetrical (3b). Why pentane substitutes: no double bond, and UV light supplies the energy (3c). Why HCl appears only in substitution: the swapped-out hydrogen leaves with the other chlorine (3c). Why the crossed pentane product fails: it loses two hydrogens (3d). Why X adds and does not substitute: no UV light (4b). Why two Cl₂ means two extra bonds: a double bond opens once (4b). Why it was one triple bond between C1 and C2, not two double bonds: every added atom is on those two carbons (4c). Why decolourisation cannot identify an alkene: alkynes add too (5b). Why the formula decides: CnH2n against CnH2n−2 (5c).
teaching.conversationalApproach: A hydrocarbon question can ask you to name a molecule, sort its isomers or predict what it makes, and each comes down to three checks (which bonds it has, what is added or swapped and under what conditions, and whether the atoms and the name check out), so every walkthrough runs those checks one step at a time. Q1 names two skeletal alkenes from the longest chain with the double bond, numbered from the end nearer it, then counts both as C6H12 and classifies them as chain isomers because the skeleton changed while both stay alkenes; Q2 adds hydrogen chloride to pent-2-ene with one piece on each carbon and two possible products, then substitutes pentane under UV light with HCl as the second product, and notes that both make a chloropentane; Q3 works backwards from 1,1,2,2-tetrachlorobutane made in the dark, where four chlorines on the same two carbons mean two additions across a triple bond, so X is but-1-yne with the atoms checked; Q4 evaluates a student's alkene conclusion from bromine water, which shows unsaturation but not which kind, so the C5H8 formula for an open-chain hydrocarbon with one multiple bond makes X an alkyne. Each question ends with its spoken, crossed classic mistake (numbering from the left, adding to an alkane, but-1-ene, bromine water as a test for double bonds only), and the decision board gives the first move for each kind of question.
teaching.openingDecision: A hydrocarbon question can ask you to name a molecule, sort its isomers, or predict what it makes. Each one here comes down to three checks. Which bonds does it have? What's added or swapped, and under what conditions? And do the atoms and the name check out? Here are four HSC-style questions. Pause and try each one, then we'll work it through, one step at a time.
teaching.understandingCheck: Four, each 10 s with the countdown and every demand and condition visible (2a, 3a, 4a, 5a): both structures (Q1); the reagents, "room temperature" and "UV light" (Q2); "excess chlorine", "in the dark", "room temperature" and the product's name and formula (Q3); the formula, the test result, the open-chain and one-multiple-bond condition, and the student's claim (Q4). Nothing answer-bearing during the holds; the check strip dims.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, p54 to 55), as printed: "investigate the nomenclature of organic chemicals, up to C8, using IUPAC conventions, including simple methyl and ethyl branched chains, including: (ACSCH127) - alkanes - alkenes - alkynes - alcohols (primary, secondary and tertiary) - aldehydes and ketones - carboxylic acids - amines and amides - halogenated organic compounds" "explore and distinguish the different types of structural isomers, including saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons, including: (ACSCH035) - chain isomers - position isomers - functional group isomers" "investigate, write equations and construct models to represent the reactions of unsaturated hydrocarbons when added to a range of chemicals, including but not limited to: - hydrogen (H2) - halogens (X2) - hydrogen halides (HX) - water (H2O) (ACSCH136)" "investigate, write equations and construct models to represent the reactions of saturated hydrocarbons when substituted with halogens" Practice and transfer only, for the parts taught so far: alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and halogenated compounds (C7-IQ1-01), hydrocarbon isomers (C7-IQ1-02), and the reactions of C7-IQ3-01 and C7-IQ3-02. The coverage rows stay with chem-m7-c01, c02, c04a and c04b; G01 adds a practice row, not first coverage. The other families in C7-IQ1-01 are practised in their own videos. starts at the route's "Read a mixed set of structures and reagents" and stops at its "Justify names, reaction types, products and conditions". Four questions, rising in demand, each with a trap: name two skeletal alkenes and classify them as isomers (numbering from the wrong end); predict the products of an alkene with HCl and an alkane with Cl₂ under UV light (adding chlorine to an alkane); work backwards from a tetrachloro product to the hydrocarbon (an alkene in place of an alkyne); evaluate a student's conclusion from a bromine water result (the test taken to prove a double bond). Each walkthrough ends with a check (count the atoms, or test the name against the structure). Not here: other families' naming (alcohols beyond the "-ol" recall, aldehydes, ketones, acids, amines, amides; their own videos); the bromine water method (chem-m7-p02, the last video); Markovnikov's rule (both possible products are accepted, as in c04a); the radical mechanism, Lindlar catalyst and alkyne hydration products (c04b Decisions); cis and trans; multi-step synthesis (chem-m7-c13 and g03); combustion.

design.visualSystem: One practice board throughout, in the chem-m6-g01 layout: top-left the question card (stem, structures or data, demand, as an exam prints them, with the tag "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience"), kept readable through the whole question; the working fills the right two thirds; a type badge top-right ("Naming and isomers", "Addition or substitution", "Working backwards", "Evaluate a test result"), hidden during each attempt where it would name the method. When the walkthrough starts, the card shrinks to a strip and each given is underlined in amber in the question text at the cue where it is used (no givens card). A check strip on the far left carries three rows, "which bonds?", "added or swapped?", "atoms and name check?", and ticks the row each scene uses; it dims to an outline during every countdown. Earlier questions are cleared before the next card writes on. Working follows the C01 to C04b staging: one structure or one equation at a time, the equation stage strip with conditions on the arrow, each earlier line dimming, kept chips for the one result the next scene needs. Colour key as chem-m7-c01 to c04b: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey; main chain pale blue (tracer); branches amber in the structure only; C=C and C≡C teal; locants small navy; chlorine green; bromine deep orange-brown; UV light violet; the HX second product boxed in thin violet. Amber in the card is used only for underlined givens. Clutter rule (owner): besides the question strip and the check strip, at most about three bright text items in the working area at once; each tag fades when the next cue lands.
design.transitionPlan: The heading writes on and four small stimulus thumbnails fan out (a skeletal zigzag, a C5H8 formula, the UV lamp and the bromine water tube) as three check chips write; each question opens on a fresh board with the type badge hidden while the worded card writes with its skeletal formulas, product formula or small unlit plate kept on screen; the walkthrough shrinks the card to a strip, lights the type badge and underlines each given in amber as the chain tracer, locant counter and name builder run, the atom tally and what-changed card write, the equation stage strip builds with the reagent splitter or swap docker, and the work-back stripper lifts chlorine pairs off as a teal triple bond returns; the bromine water tube crossfades to colourless beside ticked bond tiles and the formula lines write one per stage, earlier lines dimming to kept chips; each classic mistake writes as a chip and takes a grey scribble cross; the check strip returns full size as the two-column decision board, row by row; scene crossfade with settle.
